extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners, corporate communicators, and students designing educational/economic-education programs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for planning, producing, and evaluating educational-relations and economic-education materials and programs (K–12 through university and adult publics). Emphasizes models of communication, audience targeting, content balance, media/methods, and evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer the two-way symmetric model
rubrics_metrics.description: Only the symmetric model can truly educate people to perceive and evaluate different alternatives to complex problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programs should facilitate reciprocal dialogue between organization and publics (not simply push information). The chapter argues that organizations should enter into educational relations programs only if they practice the two-way symmetric model; other models (press agentry, one-way public information, two-way asymmetric) 'interfere with, rather than enhance, the educational process.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the press agentry model (don’t proselytize)
rubrics_metrics.description: Educational programs should not use press-agentry techniques to promote products in classrooms or to proselytize political views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern examples: Quaker Oats actor lecturing children about communism; 'Larry, the Talking Garbage Can' promoting nuclear power; programs that equivocate education with marketing. Such programs are biased, manipulative, and often inappropriate for schools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be transparent about and avoid one-sided/subsidized information
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that public relations departments provide 'subsidized information' limited to an organization's perspective and that such information often omits contrary research or competing viewpoints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing subsidized information, either avoid it for educational settings or explicitly include other perspectives and comparisons (e.g., the Chamber of Commerce should compare its view with that of environmental groups). The guidance warns that subsidized info 'does not go beyond the perspective of a single organization.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use panels of educators and advisory groups to avoid bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Involving educators and advisory panels in development helps reduce bias in materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: utilities use panels of educators and advisory groups to vet materials. Walter Purdy notes that such groups are used to avoid bias; the chapter endorses involving educators and representatives of other perspectives where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct formative research to ensure materials are appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Contract consultants or educators to do formative research on students to see that materials are appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public relations departments often contract outside consultants/educators and should require formative testing with intended student audiences before wide distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design materials to supplement and align with existing curriculum
rubrics_metrics.description: Educational relations materials should supplement existing curricular materials and be designed to fit classroom needs and levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Materials can be booklets, comic books, filmstrips, films, workbooks, or complete kits; specialists should announce materials through educational journals and sourcebooks and work with teachers to integrate them. Programs should be developed for appropriate education levels (elementary, junior high, high school, college) and may target only teachers when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place and prepare speakers to engage in genuine dialogue (not canned presentations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Speakers sent into classrooms should exchange ideas and answer questions rather than deliver canned presentations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Steel Fellows program emphasizes that fellows 'do not come to campus with canned presentations' and will work with teachers to design special programs suited to the curriculum and schedule. Speakers should represent multiple viewpoints when possible and encourage discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gather teacher evaluations and use feedback for improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect teacher evaluations and other practitioner feedback to assess material appropriateness and effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should contact teachers to acquaint them with materials, encourage use, and gather evaluations. Formal evaluation (e.g., by university research bureaus) is recommended when feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure objectives and program effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Educational relations programs should set measurable objectives and evaluate outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text references Chapter 9 for measurement techniques and notes examples of formal evaluation (e.g., University of Washington Bureau of School Service and Research evaluation of 'Project Learning Tree'). TPF&C's survey rated most materials 'fair to poor', illustrating the need for systematic evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target programs to specific publics (choose appropriate audiences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design programs with clear target publics in mind and tailor content accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TPF&C found frequent target publics in descending order: employees; the 'general' public; students; employees' families; shareholders; opinion leaders; teachers; managers; retirees; consumers; community. Program design should reflect which publics are primary and their informational needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on topics that address publics' legitimate concerns and current problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Programs should address contemporary concerns of publics (what business is doing to make the system work for them) rather than only ideological defenses of free enterprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TPF&C recommends programs be sharply focused on winning support from key constituencies and addressing legitimate concerns. Common topics listed include profits, free enterprise system, government regulation, taxation, productivity, inflation, employee benefits, competition, energy, environment, job security, product quality, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide balanced coverage of issues (do not omit relevant negatives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Educational materials should discuss both benefits and damages/risks associated with topics rather than downplaying negative consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-examples: energy materials that advocate nuclear power but 'seldom discuss the economics of constructing nuclear plants, the health effects of low-level radiation, or the problem of disposing of nuclear waste'; industry materials that downplay pollution or underplay chemical waste harms. Balanced presentation is required for true education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid stretching product-to-issue connections or misleading claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not make tenuous links between a product and educational content or obscure important facts (e.g., nutrition claims that omit sugar/additives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: McDonald's 'nutrition action pack' with branded stencils; Kellogg's Tony the Tiger posters; National Soft Drink Association booklet that touted water value of sodas but omitted sugar/additives. Such tactics reduce credibility and educational value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a variety of appropriate methods and media
rubrics_metrics.description: Select media and techniques suited to the audience and objectives (booklets, comic books, films, kits, speakers, dialogues, tours, science fairs, workshops, multimedia packages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TPF&C classified thousands of materials into categories to show the range of techniques. Examples include Telezonia (multimedia for K–6), workbooks, films, tapes, filmstrips, kits, and in-person programs like energy economics forums and multi-day dialogues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design programs to win support from and inform key constituencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Economic-education programs should be 'sharply focused' on winning support from key constituencies (especially employees and stockholders) and on addressing concerns of publics important to the sponsor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newer programs that succeed are similar to public affairs and employee relations efforts: they facilitate symmetric dialogue and aim for mutual understanding about business consequences and corrective actions.
